doc.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Firing musicians
summary: He has let people go, at least twice after recording sessions, as a last resort to keep quality up.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Did you ever have to fire anybody?

Reluctantly, yeah. Most people leave on their own, not because they’re mad or anything but they move or whatever. The only time that I let go of a couple of people was on a recording session, they couldn’t quite cut it, and it was like keep them and be faithful or look out for my reputation and all my money that I’m spending, which is thousands of dollars. So it was a rough decision but I had to do what I had to do, just to keep the quality of the music up. Also by having good musicians in the band that will attract good musicians. If you have mediocrity on comparison I’m not going to want to play with you. So I try and keep musicianship levels high so that people will want to play with me. So yes, at least two times that I can remember I let people go. I did it as tactfully as I could but you know, it is what it is. That’s why bandleaders are not popular. You’ve got to do what you’ve got to do sometimes. But I only do it as a last resort. Okay, there was one more, but we had a very bad situation, it was like okay it’s time. Because that creates, it’s like a cancer. Once it starts with somebody it can spread. That’s what somebody told me. I said something — you’re right. I’ve got to make a move here. But only as a last resort. I’m not the firing type.
